summary: AWS AI Labs presents EvalAgent, a Claude Code-based pipeline that turns an agent's source code and OTEL traces into evaluation plans, Python evaluation code (DeepEval) and reports, guided by on-demand 'evaluation skills' and Context7 API-doc retrieval. They also introduce AgentEvalBench (20 agents) and an agentic Claude Opus 4.5 meta-evaluator, and report that EvalAgent beats four Claude Code-derived baselines on pairwise preference and on Eval@1 (first-run executable, non-vacuous evaluation).

claims.evidence: Table 5(b): 17.5% is B1 (single-prompt LLM, no tools), the weakest baseline; strongest baseline B2 (Claude Code on source only) reaches 45.0-60.0% vs EvalAgent 62.5-65.0%. n=20 agents per cell, no CIs. Headline framing picks the weakest baseline.

claims.claim: Frontier coding assistants without evaluation knowledge reach only ~30% execution success and produce 12+ metrics per agent.
claims.evidence: 30% matches B3/B4 (Table 5b, Table 6) but not B2 (45-60%); '12+ metrics' matches only B4 (12.0 +/- 5.6 metric classes, Table 11) while B2/B3 average 7.1/7.2.

claims.claim: Evaluation skills are critical: removing them drops Eval@1 from 65% to ~30%, and skills keep executability stable as metric count grows.
claims.evidence: EvalAgent vs B4 (same two-stage design without skills): 62.5-65.0% vs 30.0-32.5% (Table 5b); Table 9 at 5 metrics: Ours 65%, B4 40%, B3 30% (Sonnet, n=20).

claims.claim: Up-to-date API docs via Context7 are critical for executability.
claims.evidence: Table 10: Sonnet 4.5 Eval@1 65.0% with Context7 vs 20.0% without; Haiku 62.5% vs 47.5%. Failures attributed to wrong model identifiers for DeepEval/LiteLLM/Bedrock.

claims.claim: Human experts prefer EvalAgent in 79.5% of comparisons and the meta-evaluator tracks humans.
claims.evidence: Table 3: 3 blinded annotators (no prior EvalAgent involvement, Appendix E), 40 cases EvalAgent vs B4 only, Fleiss kappa 0.923; meta-evaluator overall-winner match 39/40 but per-dimension match only 50% (Plan Quality) and 60% (Plan-Code Alignment). Rubric weights (Metric Relevance 30%, conciseness in CQC 25%, anti-length) were set heuristically by the authors and favour EvalAgent's design.

patterns.note: Skills loaded per pipeline stage with progressive disclosure; B4-vs-EvalAgent comparison isolates skills as the main driver (Table 5, Table 9).
Context7 doc retrieval (an MCP-style external resource) gives +45pp Eval@1 for Sonnet (Table 10).
Agentic LLM meta-evaluator validated against 3 humans on 40 cases: good winner agreement, weak on plan-related dimensions; generated evaluations themselves lean on LLM-as-judge metrics.
Planning without domain structure hurts (4.4x longer plans, 6.6x more code, Finding 3); planning helps only when paired with skills/templates.
OTEL/Traceloop instrumentation and trace processing are a pipeline stage; traces improve quality but reduce executability (Finding 2).
Eval@1 is an execution-based check on generated eval code, but there is no self-repair loop on first run by design.

methodology.sample: 20 agents (9 frameworks, 14 domains), 5 test scenarios and 2 requirement types each; Eval@1 cells are n=20 or 40.
methodology.baselines: B1 single-turn LLM; B2-B4 Claude Code v2.1.92 variants (source-only, +traces, +planning). All baselines are author-built ablations on the same host; no external agent-evaluation tool (e.g., stock DeepEval workflows, other hosts) compared.
methodology.models: Claude Haiku 4.5 and Sonnet 4.5 as backbones; Claude Opus 4.5 (and Sonnet 4.5) as meta-evaluator. Claude family only.
methodology.variance: Meta-evaluator run-to-run agreement reported (3 runs, 84.2% pairwise); generation results appear single-run with temperature 0 in prompts; no CIs on Eval@1.
methodology.ablations: Traces, planning, skills (via B4), Context7, metric count.
methodology.contamination_controls: None discussed; agents are public repos.
methodology.languages: Python agents and Python evaluation code (DeepEval).

standards.artifacts: Prompts and code at https://github.com/awslabs/Agent-EvalKit; AgentEvalBench described in Appendix B (release status not verified).

biases.detail: Authors built EvalAgent, AgentEvalBench, the meta-evaluator rubric (weights set heuristically) and all baselines; rubric rewards concision and few metrics, which is what EvalAgent's skills enforce.
Abstract headline 17.5% -> 65% uses the weakest baseline; '12+ metrics' and '30%' generalise from B4/B3 to 'frontier coding assistants'.
Claude family only for backbone and judge; limitations admit cross-model validation is needed.
20 agents; each Eval@1 percentage step is 5 points at n=20.
No confidence intervals or repeated generation runs for Eval@1 or win rates.
All agents and generated evaluations are Python.
Meta-evaluator only human-validated on EvalAgent vs B4 (40 cases); comparisons to B1-B3 rely on the LLM judge alone.

coi.affiliations: All 18 authors at AWS AI Labs.
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: EvalAgent (released as awslabs/Agent-EvalKit) is the authors' own system; uses Claude models (also offered via AWS Bedrock) and third-party Context7/DeepEval.
coi.detail: Vendor lab evaluating its own open-source tool on its own benchmark with its own rubric; partially mitigated by blinded human annotators with no involvement in EvalAgent, but no independent replication.

verdict_reason: Ablations (skills via B4, Context7) are informative and human validation exists, but headline numbers are framed against the weakest baseline, everything is Claude-only and Python-only at n=20, and authors own the system, benchmark and rubric.
applicability: Useful for how the team evaluates its own harness and agents rather than for Java code itself. Two transferable findings: (1) packaging domain procedure as on-demand skills/templates beat unstructured planning on the same host - analogous to shipping portable skills for ingestion conventions (schema, the domain metadata, delivery contracts) across the several repositories instead of long free-form plans; (2) live API-doc retrieval mattered most when libraries move fast - relevant for Spring/Jackson/vendor SDK versions. Caveats: Python/DeepEval-specific, Claude Code-only, so no evidence the gains hold on mixed hosts (Cursor, Codex, Hermes); the concision-favouring rubric is not a validated measure for spec-driven acceptance criteria.

conflicts_with.detail: Reports self-authored verification is unreliable in self-improving agents; EvalAgent has agents author the evaluation code and uses same-family LLMs to judge it, so its reliability claims sit in tension with that finding.
